sections.title: Stiffener Details
sections.text:
Bearing Stiffeners:
Provided at support locations to transfer reaction forces into the web. Number and spacing are configurable per member end.

Intermediate Stiffeners:
Used to improve shear resistance of slender webs. Enable and specify spacing when required.

Longitudinal Stiffeners:
Reduce web slenderness for heavily loaded girders. One or two levels can be added at 1/3 depth intervals.

Web Buckling:
Select between Simple Post Critical and Tension Field methods per IRC/IS code requirements.

sections.title: Permanent Loads
sections.text:
Dead loads are divided into the following categories:

SW — Self-weight of the girder. The self-weight modification factor entered by the user is multiplied with this case to account for connections and accessories not explicitly modelled.
DC — Weight of structural steel components other than the girder, including cross bracing and end diaphragms.
DD — Weight of the concrete deck slab.
DW — Weight of the wearing course (surfacing) applied on the deck.
SIDL — Superimposed Dead Load, comprising crash barriers, median, and railings.

All load magnitudes are computed internally from member dimensions and material densities. The self-weight modification factor (SW) is the only user-controlled parameter for this load group.

sections.title: Live Load (LL)
sections.text:
IRC Vehicles:
Live load considers standard IRC 6 vehicle classes: Class A, Class 70R (Wheeled, Tracked, Bogie), Class AA (Wheeled, Tracked), Class SV (Special Vehicle), and Fatigue vehicle. Only checked vehicles are included in the analysis.

Braking Load (IRC 6 Cl. 211.2):
Braking forces are derived from the live load. For single- or two-lane bridges: 20% of the first train of load plus 10% of succeeding trains in one lane.
For bridges with more than two lanes: as above for the first two lanes, plus 5% for each additional lane.
Class SV does not require a braking load by default, but a checkbox is provided if the user wishes to include it.

Braking Load Eccentricity:
As per IRC 6, braking load acts as a horizontal longitudinal force applied at 1.2 m above the top of the deck surface.

Footpath Pressure:
Footpath live load is applied as a uniform pressure per IRC 6. The default value follows the code; the user can switch to 'User-defined' to enter a custom value.

sections.title: Seismic / Earthquake Load (EL)
sections.text:
Seismic zone is auto-filled from the project location and determines the zone factor (Z) per IRC 6.

Spectral acceleration coefficient (Sa/g) is taken from IRC 6 response spectra and depends on the soil type and the fundamental time period (T) of the structure.

Seismic coefficients:
Ah = (Z / 2) x (I / R) x (Sa/g)
Av = (2/3) x Ah
where Z = zone factor, I = importance factor, R = response reduction factor, and the damping percentage governs the Sa/g value. All calculations follow IRC 6 seismic provisions.

sections.title: Wind Load (WL)
sections.text:
Basic wind speed is auto-filled from the project location.

Hourly mean wind speed (Vz) and design wind pressure (Pz) are computed from the basic wind speed, average exposed height (H), terrain type, and site topography per IRC 6.

Wind forces computed per IRC 6 include:
- Transverse wind force on the structure
- Longitudinal wind force (typically 25% of transverse)
- Vertical (upward) wind force on the deck
- Transverse and longitudinal wind forces due to live load

These forces use the gust factor (G), drag coefficient (CD), lift coefficient (CL), superstructure elevation area, plan area, and exposed frontal area of live load. They are applied at the specified eccentricity or as required by IRC 6.

sections.title: Temperature Load (TL)
sections.text:
Highest maximum and lowest minimum air shade temperatures are auto-filled from the project location (per IRC 6 Annex B meteorological data).

Coefficient of thermal expansion (α):
Governs the unit change in length per degree Celsius. IRC 6 Cl. 215 specifies 12 × 10⁻⁶ /°C for steel and 12 × 10⁻⁶ /°C for RCC; values may be revised if site-specific material data is available. Both coefficients are user-editable.

Range of effective bridge temperature (EBT):
The effective bridge temperature is the uniform temperature through the depth of the bridge cross-section at any instant. The minimum and maximum EBT values are derived from the air shade temperatures using IRC 6 Cl. 215. These are computed automatically and shown read-only.

Temperature for design:
• Temperature Rise = Maximum EBT − Mean temperature
• Temperature Fall = Mean temperature − Minimum EBT
The Mean temperature is the midpoint of min and max air shade temperatures. The rise and fall values are used to compute thermal expansion and contraction forces, and longitudinal effects throughout the analysis.

sections.title: Load Combinations (IRC 6)
sections.text:
Load combinations are formed per IRC 6 Table B.1. The following load cases are considered:
SW: Self-weight of steel girder
DC: Weight of structural steel components other than the girder, including cross bracing and end diaphragms
DD: Deck weight
DW: Wearing course
SIDL: Crash barriers, median, railing
LL: Live load
WL: Wind load
EL: Seismic / earthquake load
TL: Temperature load

IRC 6 combination types:
- Basic combination
- Accidental combination
- Seismic combination
- Frequent combination
- Rare combination
- Quasi-permanent combination

Custom load combinations with user-defined partial safety factors can also be added.

sections.title: Construction Stages
sections.text:
When included ('Yes'), the analysis accounts for three stages.
In Stage 1, the steel girder carries its self-weight alone.
In Stage 2, the wet concrete deck load (DD) and the weight of other structural steel components act on the bare steel section before composite action is activated.
In Stage 3, composite action is fully active, and all remaining loads (superimposed dead load, live load, wind load, seismic load, and temperature load) are applied to the composite section.
Stages 1 and 2 are critical for lateral-torsional buckling (LTB) checks, as the compression flange is unrestrained until the deck provides lateral support.

When 'No' is selected, only the final composite state is checked and no separate construction-stage verification is performed.
